experiences.title: Prophet William Wadé Harris and the Ivorian mass movement
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Harris's statements recorded by visitors and of David Shank's reconstruction: while imprisoned in Liberia for political activity (1910), the Grebo teacher William Wadé Harris received a visit from the angel Gabriel, who called him to be a prophet, to burn fetishes and to baptise. From 1913 to 1915, dressed in a white robe with a cross-topped staff, a Bible and a calabash rattle, he walked along the coast of the French Ivory Coast and the Gold Coast, preaching against traditional 'fetishes', baptising perhaps 100,000-120,000 people, and directing converts to wait for teachers 'with the Bible'.

primarySource.title: Accounts collected by missionaries and administrators (e.g. Methodist missionary reports, 1914-1926)
primarySource.citation: Testimonies gathered by W.J. Platt and others; Harris's 1926 interview with Pierre Benoit

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: French colonial authorities expelled Harris in 1915, fearing unrest. When Methodist missionaries arrived in 1924 they found thousands of Harris converts awaiting them; others formed the independent Harrist Church.

assessments.text: Harris is honoured as a prophet of African Christianity who preached in an indigenous idiom, accepted polygamy among converts, and empowered African agency.
Mission churches in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana grew directly from his movement; Methodists honour his evangelistic role while distancing themselves from some practices.
Seen as a forerunner of African Pentecostalism's emphasis on power encounter, healing and deliverance from spirits.
Lamin Sanneh, Adrian Hastings and David Shank use Harris as a key case of African-led Christianisation outpacing Western missions.

debates: Power encounter and the burning of traditional objects.
experiences.story:
William Wadé Harris was born around 1860 among the Grebo people near Cape Palmas in south-eastern Liberia, a country then dominated politically by the Americo-Liberian elite descended from freed African Americans. As a boy he lived with a Methodist minister and was converted; as a young man he worked as a seaman on ships along the West African coast. He later became a teacher and catechist in the Protestant Episcopal (Anglican) mission and served as a government interpreter. Like many Grebo, he resented Americo-Liberian rule, and in 1909 he was arrested for his part in a pro-British political movement among the Grebo, including the raising of a British flag.

In prison in 1910, according to what Harris later told visitors, the angel Gabriel appeared to him in a trance and called him to be a prophet of the last days. He was told to abandon his European clothes, to preach Christ, to destroy fetishes, the objects used in traditional religion, and to baptise. During his imprisonment his wife Rose died. After his release he dressed in a white gown and turban, carried a bamboo cross-topped staff, a Bible and a calabash rattle, and set out to preach, at first with little success in Liberia.

In mid-1913 Harris crossed into the French colony of the Ivory Coast, accompanied by women singers, and walked eastward along the coast and lagoons. His message was simple: give up fetishes and traditional spirit practices, worship the one God, keep Sunday, avoid alcohol and adultery, and be baptised. According to colonial and missionary reports, whole villages responded. People brought their traditional objects to be burned, and Harris baptised them by sprinkling water on their heads from a bowl, sometimes laying his Bible on them. Witnesses reported healings, and stories circulated of sudden misfortunes befalling those who mocked him.

He went on into the British Gold Coast (Ghana) as far as the Axim and Apollonia region in 1914, then returned to the Ivory Coast lagoons. Unlike most missionaries he did not require converts to give up polygamous marriages, which he himself practised, and he did not build a church organisation of his own. Instead he told converts to build chapels, appoint leaders, and wait for teachers who would come 'with the Bible'; some villages appointed twelve 'apostles' to lead them. Within about eighteen months he had baptised, by most estimates, between 100,000 and 120,000 people.

The French colonial authorities, at war in Europe from August 1914 and alarmed by a mass movement under an African prophet from British-influenced Liberia, arrested Harris and expelled him in early 1915. Many of the chapels his converts built were destroyed and some of his followers were persecuted. Harris returned to Liberia, where he continued to preach on a smaller scale until his death in 1929.

When British Methodist missionaries led by William J. Platt reached the Ivory Coast in 1924, they found tens of thousands of Harris's converts still meeting and waiting for teachers, and they absorbed many of them into the Methodist Church. Catholic missions also grew. In 1926 Platt sent Pierre Benoît to visit Harris in Liberia; Benoît brought back a statement which the Methodists presented as Harris's endorsement. Other converts, who rejected the missions' rules on polygamy and wanted an African-led church, formed the Harrist Church, organised by John Ahui, which is still active in Côte d'Ivoire.

keyMoments.text: William Wadé Harris is born, around this year, among the Grebo near Cape Palmas, Liberia.
He is arrested for his part in a pro-British political movement among the Grebo.
In prison he reports a visit from the angel Gabriel calling him to be a prophet.
Harris crosses into the Ivory Coast and begins preaching, burning fetishes and baptising.
He extends his mission into the Gold Coast, reaching the Axim and Apollonia region.
French authorities expel him after he has baptised perhaps 100,000-120,000 people.
Methodist missionaries led by William J. Platt find thousands of Harris converts awaiting teachers.
Harris dies in Liberia; the independent Harrist Church develops in the following years.

experiences.significance: Harris led what is often described as the largest mass movement to Christianity in West African history up to that time, achieved in under two years by an African prophet without missionary support. His career is a classic case of African agency in the spread of Christianity, a theme emphasised by scholars such as Lamin Sanneh and Andrew Walls. His ministry seeded Methodist and Catholic growth in Côte d'Ivoire and Ghana and inspired African-initiated churches such as the Harrist Church and the Church of the Twelve Apostles in Ghana. It also raises lasting questions about power encounters with traditional religion, polygamy and church discipline, and the colonial suppression of African prophets.

experiences.title: Simon Kimbangu's healing ministry at Nkamba
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Kimbanguist tradition and colonial and Baptist mission records: in April 1921 the Baptist catechist Simon Kimbangu, who had resisted earlier calls he believed came from Christ, laid hands on a sick woman who was reported healed. For about five months crowds flocked to his village of Nkamba seeking healing; he preached against fetishes and polygamy and in favour of Bible reading. Belgian authorities, alarmed by the movement and by workers leaving their jobs, arrested him in September 1921; his death sentence was commuted to life imprisonment, and he died in prison in Élisabethville (Lubumbashi) in 1951.

primarySource.title: Records of the Baptist Missionary Society and Belgian colonial trial documents (1921)
primarySource.citation: Marie-Louise Martin, Kimbangu: An African Prophet and His Church (1975), drawing on oral and archival sources

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Colonial officials saw a political threat; Baptist missionaries were divided. The movement survived underground and was legally recognised in 1959 as the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth by His Messenger Simon Kimbangu (EJCSK), which joined the World Council of Churches in 1969.

assessments.text: Kimbangu is God's messenger and Nkamba is the 'New Jerusalem'; his suffering is seen as Christlike. Later Kimbanguist teaching attributed elevated spiritual status to Kimbangu and his descendants.
Many recognised a genuine evangelistic movement but have voiced concerns about later doctrinal developments regarding the Kimbangu family.
Seen as an early African healing revival, comparable to Harris and the Aladura.
Historians emphasise its anticolonial significance in Belgian Congo and its role as a model of African Christian independence.

debates: Later Christological teaching about Kimbangu and orthodoxy.
experiences.story:
Simon Kimbangu was born in the late 1880s at Nkamba in the Lower Congo, among the BaKongo people, in what was then the Congo Free State and from 1908 the Belgian Congo. The region had endured the brutality of the Free State's rubber regime, and colonial rule weighed heavily through forced labour and taxation. Kimbangu was educated at the English Baptist Missionary Society station at Ngombe Lutete, baptised with his wife Marie Mwilu around 1915, and served as a catechist.

According to Kimbanguist tradition, during the influenza epidemic of 1918 he heard a call he believed came from Christ to care for the sick and preach. He resisted, feeling unworthy, and went to work in Léopoldville (Kinshasa), but the call continued. Tradition holds that on 6 April 1921 he laid hands on a sick woman in a neighbouring village and she was healed. The date is still celebrated by his followers.

News spread with remarkable speed. For about five months thousands of people came to Nkamba, which followers began to call the 'New Jerusalem', seeking healing. Kimbangu prayed for the sick, preached repentance, called people to abandon fetishes and traditional charms, condemned polygamy and dancing, and urged Bible reading and faith in God. Colonial and mission sources report that hospitals and mission stations emptied, and that workers left plantations and other employment to go to Nkamba. Other 'prophets' (bangunza) appeared in the region, some with more overtly anti-colonial messages.

Belgian officials and businesses grew alarmed, fearing a political uprising and economic disruption. Baptist missionaries were divided: some initially saw the movement as a genuine revival, while others worried about excess and their loss of control, and the Catholic missions were hostile. In June 1921 an attempt to arrest Kimbangu failed and he went into hiding. On 12 September 1921, according to his followers, he gave himself up voluntarily.

A military court at Thysville in October 1921 convicted him of endangering state security and sentenced him to death and 120 lashes. After appeals, including from Baptist missionaries, the Belgian King Albert commuted the sentence to life imprisonment. Kimbangu was transported to Élisabethville (Lubumbashi) in the far south of the colony, where he remained in prison for about thirty years until his death on 12 October 1951. Thousands of his followers were deported to remote parts of the colony, which unintentionally spread the movement.

The movement survived underground for decades despite repression. In 1959, shortly before Congolese independence, the Belgian authorities granted legal recognition to the Church of Jesus Christ on Earth by His Messenger the Prophet Simon Kimbangu (EJCSK), led by his youngest son Joseph Diangienda. The church grew into one of the largest African-initiated churches, with millions of members, built a great temple at Nkamba, and joined the World Council of Churches in 1969. In later decades some of its teachings about the divine status of Kimbangu and his descendants raised serious questions from other churches about its theological orthodoxy.

keyMoments.text: Simon Kimbangu and his wife Marie Mwilu are baptised at the Baptist mission at Ngombe Lutete.
During the influenza epidemic Kimbangu reports a call to heal and preach, which he at first resists.
According to tradition, he lays hands on a sick woman who is healed, beginning his public ministry.
Crowds flock to Nkamba for healing; colonial authorities grow alarmed.
Kimbangu surrenders to the authorities after months in hiding.
A military court sentences him to death; King Albert later commutes the sentence to life imprisonment.
Kimbangu dies in prison in Élisabethville after some thirty years' captivity.
The Kimbanguist Church (EJCSK) receives legal recognition under Joseph Diangienda.
The Kimbanguist Church joins the World Council of Churches.

experiences.significance: Kimbangu's brief ministry founded what became one of the largest African-initiated churches, and he is honoured in the Democratic Republic of Congo as a national figure who suffered under colonial rule. His story became a powerful symbol of African Christian independence and of the colonial suppression of African prophets, and historians use it to explore the interplay of religion, healing and resistance. The church's entry into the World Council of Churches was a landmark in the recognition of African-initiated churches by older denominations. At the same time, later Kimbanguist teaching on the divinity of Kimbangu and his sons has led many other Christians to question whether the church remains within historic Trinitarian orthodoxy.

experiences.title: Aladura revival and Joseph Babalola at Ilesa
experiences.account: Paraphrase of J.D.Y. Peel's reconstruction and church histories: Aladura ('people of prayer') groups arose in Yorubaland during the 1918 influenza epidemic, when Anglican members of the Precious Stone/Faith Tabernacle prayer society relied on prayer and blessed water. In July 1930, Joseph Ayo Babalola, a former steamroller driver who had reported a call in a vision (1928), began a revival at Oke-Oye, Ilesa: crowds came for healing by prayer and water, traditional objects were burned and thousands converted. Similar prophet-led churches include the Cherubim and Seraphim (from 1925) and the Church of the Lord (Aladura) (1930).

primarySource.title: Church histories of the Christ Apostolic Church; colonial and missionary reports (1930-31)
primarySource.citation: J.D.Y. Peel, Aladura: A Religious Movement among the Yoruba (1968)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Colonial authorities and mission churches were uneasy about mass healing meetings and conflict with the use of medicine; Babalola was briefly imprisoned in 1932 in connection with witch-finding activities. The movement led to the Christ Apostolic Church (1941), after a split with British Apostolic Church missionaries over the use of medicine.

assessments.text: The revival is a foundational sign of God's power in Africa; prayer, visions, fasting and holy water are central to worship.
Historically critical of rejection of medicine and syncretism concerns, while today acknowledging the Aladura as authentic African Christianity.
African Pentecostals see Aladura as forerunners, though newer Pentecostal churches often criticise Aladura use of candles, water and robes as syncretistic.
Peel interprets Aladura as a Yoruba search for power and well-being expressed in Christian form during colonial upheaval.

experiences.story:
In the early twentieth century south-western Nigeria, Yorubaland, was under British colonial rule, with Anglican, Methodist, Baptist and Catholic missions well established. In 1918 the global influenza pandemic struck hard. At St Saviour's Anglican Church in Ijebu-Ode, a group led by J.B. Shadare and the young woman Sophia Odunlami, claiming guidance through dreams and visions, formed a prayer circle that relied on prayer rather than medicine for healing. It became known as the Precious Stone (or Diamond) Society. Its members rejected both traditional medicine and Western medical treatment, and when the Anglican Church objected, the group left and affiliated in the 1920s with Faith Tabernacle, an American faith-healing church based in Philadelphia, through its magazine.

Joseph Ayo Babalola was born in 1904 and worked as a steamroller driver for the colonial Public Works Department. According to the Christ Apostolic Church's histories, in October 1928, while working on a road, he heard a voice calling him to leave his job and preach, and he received a vision commissioning him to pray for the sick using water blessed by prayer. He resigned, joined the Faith Tabernacle in Lagos, and began to preach.

In July 1930 Faith Tabernacle leaders gathered at Oke-Oye in Ilesa for a meeting. According to the church's tradition, during this gathering Babalola prayed for a dead boy who was then restored to life. Whatever the event, it marked the beginning of a mass movement. For weeks huge crowds came to Ilesa and then to other towns in Yoruba and Ekiti country to hear him preach and to be prayed for. People brought charms and traditional ritual objects to be burned, drank or washed in water he had prayed over, and testified to healings, especially of barrenness, blindness and lameness. Thousands were baptised. Missionaries and colonial officials reported that some mission churches lost members to the new movement.

Colonial authorities and mission churches watched with concern. They objected to the rejection of medicine and to fears of witchcraft accusations; in 1932 Babalola was imprisoned for some months in connection with witch-finding activities associated with the revival. Meanwhile the Faith Tabernacle leaders, seeking stronger links abroad, invited missionaries from the British Apostolic Church, a Pentecostal denomination based in Wales; they arrived in 1931. For several years the Nigerian movement and the British Pentecostals worked together, bringing Pentecostal teaching on Spirit baptism and tongues into the Yoruba revival.

Tensions grew, especially over medicine: some British missionaries used quinine against malaria, while many Nigerian leaders insisted on total reliance on prayer. Around 1939-40 the movement split. The British-linked group continued as the Apostolic Church, and Babalola and his Nigerian colleagues formed what was registered in the early 1940s as the Christ Apostolic Church, one of the largest indigenous Pentecostal churches in Nigeria. Babalola continued to preach until his death in 1959.

Alongside these developments other Aladura ('owners of prayer') churches arose, notably the Cherubim and Seraphim, founded in Lagos in 1925 by Moses Orimolade Tunolase and Christiana Abiodun Akinsowon, and the Church of the Lord (Aladura), founded by Josiah Oshitelu in 1930. They shared an emphasis on prayer, healing, visions and the struggle against evil spiritual powers, expressed in Yoruba forms of worship.

keyMoments.text: During the influenza pandemic a prayer group at St Saviour's Anglican Church, Ijebu-Ode, begins healing by prayer alone.
The Cherubim and Seraphim movement is founded in Lagos by Moses Orimolade and Christiana Abiodun Akinsowon.
Steamroller driver Joseph Ayo Babalola reports a divine call and leaves his job to preach.
At Oke-Oye, Ilesa, Babalola begins a mass healing revival; crowds burn traditional objects.
Missionaries of the British Apostolic Church arrive at the invitation of Nigerian Faith Tabernacle leaders.
Babalola is imprisoned for some months in connection with witch-finding associated with the revival.
A split over the use of medicine leads Babalola's group to form what becomes the Christ Apostolic Church.
Babalola dies; the Christ Apostolic Church remains one of Nigeria's largest indigenous churches.

experiences.significance: The Aladura movement and Babalola's revival created some of the first and largest African-initiated Pentecostal-type churches, and they helped set the pattern for Nigerian Christianity, now among the most vibrant in the world and a major exporter of churches to Europe and North America. They showed African Christians shaping the faith around their own concerns, especially healing, protection from evil powers and prophecy, which scholars such as J.D.Y. Peel and Lamin Sanneh interpret as genuine inculturation. Critics, including mission churches at the time, raised concerns about the rejection of medicine, witch-finding, and possible syncretism with traditional religion. Babalola is honoured today with a university and an annual pilgrimage at Ikeji-Arakeji.

experiences.title: The East African Revival (Balokole)
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Joe Church's memoir and later histories: after the Ugandan layman Simeon Nsibambi and the English missionary doctor Joe Church met in Kampala in 1929 and studied the Bible together, a revival broke out at the Gahini mission in Rwanda in 1933, then spread through Uganda, Kenya and Tanganyika. Its marks were conviction of sin, public confession, restitution and 'walking in the light' in fellowship. Some meetings in the 1930s saw people trembling, weeping and having visions, which leaders came to downplay.

primarySource.title: J.E. (Joe) Church, Quest for the Highest: An Autobiographical Account of the East African Revival (1981)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: The revival largely stayed within the Anglican Church, though at times it clashed with clergy who found the Balokole ('saved ones') judgemental. During the Mau Mau emergency (1950s) many revivalists refused to take oaths and were killed, which gave the movement moral prestige.

assessments.text: A formative renewal shaping East African Anglicanism and leaders such as Archbishop Janani Luwum and Festo Kivengere.
Sometimes claimed as a precursor, though the revival mainly avoided tongues and sought order within the established church.
Kevin Ward and Emma Wild-Wood stress its African leadership, interracial fellowship (Brethren) and its tensions with both mission and nationalist politics.
Public confession created strong community bonds and moral accountability, but some critics noted pressure and perfectionism.

experiences.story:
In the 1920s the Church Missionary Society's Ruanda Mission, an evangelical Anglican mission rooted in the Keswick 'victorious life' tradition, opened stations in south-western Uganda and in Rwanda, then under Belgian mandate. At Gahini, on the eastern side of Rwanda, the mission ran a hospital and schools. Joe Church, a young English doctor from Cambridge, arrived there in 1927. In 1928-29 a severe famine struck Rwanda, and Church, exhausted and discouraged by the gap between the missionaries' message and the lives of many church members, travelled to Kampala in September 1929 for a break.

In Kampala he met Simeon Nsibambi, a Ugandan layman and government official known for his serious piety. According to Church's memoir, the two spent days studying the Bible together on the Holy Spirit and the victorious Christian life, and both reported a deep personal renewal. Nsibambi began to challenge fellow Christians in Kampala about sin and new life, and Church returned to Gahini with a new message.

Over the next few years a small group formed at Gahini, including Blasio Kigozi, Nsibambi's younger brother, a teacher at the mission, and Yosiya Kinuka, a hospital assistant. They met for prayer and Bible study and confessed sins to one another. In late 1933 and early 1934, according to Church and others, revival broke out at Gahini: people came under strong conviction of sin, wept, confessed publicly, and some trembled, cried out or had visions. Restitution followed: stolen goods were returned and enemies reconciled. Kigozi preached urgently to the church in Uganda but died of fever in January 1936.

Teams of Africans and Europeans, including Church, Nsibambi, William Nagenda and later Festo Kivengere, carried the message by conventions and visits through Uganda, Kenya, Tanganyika, Burundi and beyond. The movement's members came to be called the Balokole, 'the saved ones'. Their marks were open confession of sin, 'walking in the light' with one another in small fellowship groups, a strong emphasis on the cross and the blood of Jesus, simple living, and the hymn 'Tukutendereza Yesu' ('We praise you, Jesus'). Leaders came to discourage dramatic physical manifestations in favour of quiet brokenness and repentance.

The revival largely remained within the Anglican Church and other Protestant churches, but tensions were frequent. Clergy sometimes found the Balokole judgemental, separatist or contemptuous of church order, and revivalists criticised what they saw as nominal Christianity and compromise. In 1941 students at Bishop Tucker College, Mukono, were expelled after a dispute in which revivalists protested against what they saw as liberal teaching. Many Balokole also challenged ethnic and racial barriers, insisting that Europeans and Africans meet as equals in fellowship.

The movement's most dramatic test came in Kenya during the Mau Mau emergency of the 1950s. Many revival Christians among the Kikuyu refused to take Mau Mau oaths, which they saw as incompatible with their faith, while also refusing to take up arms for the colonial government; some were killed for their refusal. Their witness, combined with their opposition to colonial violence, gave the revival moral authority. The revival continued as a powerful current into the post-independence period, shaping leaders such as Archbishop Janani Luwum of Uganda, murdered under Idi Amin in 1977.

keyMoments.text: Dr Joe Church joins the CMS Ruanda Mission at Gahini, Rwanda.
Church meets Simeon Nsibambi in Kampala; their Bible study together brings both a deep renewal.
Revival breaks out at Gahini, with conviction of sin, public confession and restitution.
Blasio Kigozi, a leading early voice of the revival, dies of fever.
Revival teams hold conventions in Kenya, extending the movement across East Africa.
Revivalist students are expelled from Bishop Tucker College, Mukono, after a theological dispute.
During the Mau Mau emergency many Kenyan revivalists refuse oaths, and some are killed.
Archbishop Janani Luwum, shaped by the revival, is murdered under Idi Amin.

experiences.significance: The East African Revival is one of the longest-lasting and most influential revival movements in modern Christianity, shaping Anglican and Protestant churches in Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi, Kenya and Tanzania for decades and producing many of their leaders. It showed that revival could remain within an established church while renewing it through lay fellowship groups and African leadership, and its practice of mutual confession and reconciliation across racial lines was striking in colonial Africa. Critics have pointed to legalism, spiritual elitism and tendencies to schism, and later observers have asked why such a strong revival tradition did not prevent the violence of Rwanda in 1994. Its influence continues in East African Anglicanism and in global evangelical networks.

experiences.title: Sadhu Sundar Singh's vision of Christ
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Sundar Singh's own testimony as recorded by Streeter and Appasamy: a fifteen-year-old Sikh boy, grieving his mother's death and hostile to Christianity (he publicly burned a Bible), prayed through the night of 18 December 1904 resolved to die on the railway line before the morning train unless God revealed himself. Before dawn a light filled his room and he saw the figure of Jesus with nail-pierced hands, who spoke to him in Hindustani. Baptised in the Anglican church in Shimla in 1905, he became a wandering Christian sadhu in saffron robes, travelling across India and into Tibet.

primarySource.title: B.H. Streeter and A.J. Appasamy, The Sadhu: A Study in Mysticism and Practical Religion (1921)
primarySource.citation: Streeter & Appasamy 1921; Sundar Singh's own writings, e.g. At the Master's Feet (1922)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: His vision and ascetic Indian style made him famous in Europe in the 1920s. He disappeared on a journey into Tibet in 1929. Some European critics (the Jesuit Fr Hosten and the psychoanalyst Oskar Pfister, 1926) questioned miracle stories in his travels, such as a 300-year-old 'Maharishi of Kailash'.

assessments.text: Celebrated as a pioneer of indigenous Indian Christianity who showed that faith in Christ need not mean Westernisation.
Respected as a mystic; some Catholic critics in his day investigated and disputed specific miracle claims.
His visions are often cited as examples of direct revelation of Christ to people of other faiths, a theme recurring in reports from the Muslim world.
Pfister's psychoanalytic study and later scholars debate how to read his visions; his conversion account is consistent and first-hand, while the later travel miracles are less corroborated.

experiences.story:
Sundar Singh was born in 1889 into a wealthy Sikh family in the village of Rampur, in the Ludhiana district of the Punjab. His mother was deeply religious and took him to Sikh holy places and to Hindu ascetics (sadhus), and he learned scriptures from Sikh and Hindu traditions. He also attended a school run by American Presbyterian missionaries, where the Bible was taught, which he resented.

When he was fourteen his mother died, and he was overwhelmed by grief and spiritual restlessness. According to his own later account, in his anger he tore up and publicly burned a copy of the Gospels, and he threw stones at Christian preachers. In December 1904, he said, he resolved to find peace or die: he would pray through the night, and if God did not reveal himself by morning he would throw himself in front of the early train that passed near his home.

On the night of 18 December 1904 he prayed, according to his testimony, to whatever God might exist. Before dawn, he said, a bright light filled the room, and he saw the figure of Jesus, whom he recognised from pictures and from the Gospels, with the marks of the nails in his hands. He reported that Jesus spoke to him in Hindustani, asking why he persecuted him, and that he was filled with peace. He woke his father and told him he had become a follower of Jesus.

His family tried to dissuade him with persuasion, inducements and threats. According to his account, he was eventually driven from home, and food given to him on his departure had been poisoned, from which he recovered with the help of Christians. He went to the mission at Ludhiana, and on his sixteenth birthday, 3 September 1905, he was baptised at St Thomas's Anglican Church in Shimla.

Soon afterwards he adopted the saffron robe of a Hindu sadhu, believing that Indians would better understand Christ through a familiar form of holy life. He travelled on foot through the Punjab, Kashmir and the Himalayas, owning almost nothing, and repeatedly crossed into Tibet, where Christian preaching was forbidden. He briefly studied at St John's Divinity College in Lahore and received a preaching licence, but later gave it up to remain free of denominational ties. Stories circulated, many from his own lips, of persecution and miraculous deliverance in Tibet, including being thrown into a dry well and rescued by an unknown helper, and of meeting a Christian hermit hundreds of years old, the 'Maharishi of Kailash'.

From 1918 he made speaking tours across India, Ceylon, Malaya, China and Japan, and in 1920 and 1922 visited Britain, the United States, Australia and continental Europe, where large audiences were drawn by his calm, simple teaching and parable-like style. The theologian B.H. Streeter and A.J. Appasamy published a study of his spirituality in 1921, and his own short books, such as At the Master's Feet, were widely translated. Controversy followed: in the mid-1920s the Jesuit H. Hosten and the Swiss pastor and psychoanalyst Oskar Pfister argued that some of his travel and miracle stories were unverified or untrue, while the scholar Friedrich Heiler defended him. In April 1929 Sundar Singh set out once more for Tibet and was never seen again.

keyMoments.text: Sundar Singh is born into a Sikh family in Rampur, Punjab.
His mother dies; in grief he becomes hostile to Christianity and burns a copy of the Gospels.
He prays through the night, resolved to die unless God reveals himself, and reports a vision of Jesus before dawn.
After rejection by his family, he is baptised at St Thomas's Anglican Church, Shimla.
He adopts the saffron robe of a sadhu and begins wandering as a Christian ascetic preacher.
He tours Britain and the United States, attracting wide attention.
Oskar Pfister and H. Hosten publish critiques questioning some of his miracle stories.
He sets out for Tibet and disappears.

experiences.significance: Sadhu Sundar Singh became the best-known Indian Christian of his generation and a pioneer of expressing faith in Christ through Indian forms of holiness rather than European church culture, an approach later developed in Indian Christian ashrams and theology. His conversion through a vision, without human preaching, is frequently cited in discussions of dreams and visions of Christ among people of other faiths. The controversy over his travel stories made him a test case for evaluating testimony and hagiography in modern times. He remains widely read in India and beyond, and is commemorated in some Anglican calendars.

experiences.title: John Sung's revival and healing campaigns in China and Southeast Asia
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Sung's diaries and Lian Xi's study: John Sung (Song Shangjie), a Fujianese pastor's son with a PhD in chemistry from Ohio State University, experienced a dramatic conversion in New York in 1927 and was confined for six months in a psychiatric hospital before returning to China. From 1931 with the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band, and independently from 1933, he preached across China and among Chinese in the Philippines, Malaya, Singapore and the Dutch East Indies until about 1940, with intense calls to repentance, dramatic gestures and healing services in which thousands reported cures.

primarySource.title: John Sung's diaries (published in Chinese as The Diaries of John Sung, ed. Levi Sung, 1995)
primarySource.citation: Lian Xi, Redeemed by Fire (2010); Leslie Lyall, A Biography of John Sung (1954)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Admirers called him the 'Wesley of China'; Chinese Christians credited him with planting hundreds of preaching bands. Critics, including some missionaries, disliked his harshness and theatrical methods. He died of tuberculosis in 1944.

assessments.text: A spiritual father of independent Chinese Protestantism whose emphasis on repentance, Bible and evangelistic bands influenced later house churches.
Some missionaries criticised his anti-modernist polemics and emotional style but acknowledged his effectiveness.
Lian Xi places Sung within the rise of an indigenous, millenarian popular Protestantism in Republican China.
His 1927 hospitalisation is variously read as a breakdown, a misunderstood conversion crisis or both.

experiences.story:
John Sung (Song Shangjie) was born in 1901 in Hinghwa (Putian), Fujian province, the son of a Methodist pastor. As a boy he was affected by a local revival in 1909 and became known as a 'little pastor' for his preaching. In 1919 he went to the United States to study, earning degrees at Ohio Wesleyan University and Ohio State University, where he received a PhD in chemistry in 1926. He then enrolled at Union Theological Seminary in New York, where liberal theology threw his faith into crisis.

According to his diaries, in February 1927, after a period of spiritual turmoil, he experienced an intense conversion: a vision of Christ, a sense of total forgiveness, and a call to preach. His behaviour became so extreme, including fervent public preaching and declarations that alarmed the seminary, that he was committed to a psychiatric hospital in New York, where he remained for about six months. He later described this as a time of deep Bible study. After his release he sailed for China in late 1927; according to a well-known story, he threw his academic certificates into the sea, keeping only his doctoral diploma for his father.

Back in Fujian he taught and preached, and in 1931 he joined the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band, organised by the Bethel Mission in Shanghai, a mission led by the American missionary Jennie Hughes and the Chinese physician Mary Stone (Shi Meiyu). With Andrew Gih (Ji Zhiwen) and others, the band travelled thousands of miles across China, holding revival meetings in churches of many denominations. In 1933-34 Sung parted from Bethel and continued independently.

His preaching was unforgettable. Witnesses describe him running across the platform, using props such as a coffin to illustrate death to sin, singing songs he had composed, and naming specific sins of church members and pastors, demanding public confession and restitution. Meetings often lasted many hours over several days. Healing services became part of his campaigns: he prayed over long lines of sick people, and thousands reported cures. He organised converts into 'preaching bands' of three or more lay people who went out weekly to evangelise, and emphasised Bible study.

From 1935 he travelled extensively among the Chinese diaspora of South-East Asia, in the Philippines, Singapore, Malaya, Thailand, Taiwan and the Dutch East Indies, where many churches date their growth to his visits. Critics, including some missionaries and Chinese church leaders, objected to his harshness, his public attacks on clergy, his emotionalism and his theatrical methods; some questioned the healing claims. The historian Lian Xi has analysed him as a central figure in the rise of a fervent, independent Chinese Christianity with apocalyptic and charismatic tendencies.

By 1940 his health was failing from tuberculosis and other illness, and he spent his final years largely bedridden in Beijing, writing and praying, during the Japanese occupation. He died on 18 August 1944, aged 42.

keyMoments.text: John Sung is born in Hinghwa (Putian), Fujian, the son of a Methodist pastor.
He receives a PhD in chemistry from Ohio State University and enters Union Theological Seminary.
He reports a dramatic conversion and is soon committed to a psychiatric hospital for about six months.
Sung returns to China, reportedly discarding his diplomas at sea except his doctorate.
He joins the Bethel Worldwide Evangelistic Band and begins nationwide revival tours.
He leaves Bethel and continues as an independent evangelist.
He begins campaigns among overseas Chinese across South-East Asia.
Sung dies in Beijing after years of illness.

experiences.significance: John Sung is widely regarded as the most influential Chinese evangelist of the twentieth century, and his campaigns in China and South-East Asia shaped generations of Chinese churches, preachers and lay preaching bands. His fervent, Bible-centred and often charismatic style foreshadowed the independent Chinese Christianity that later grew in house churches after missionaries left. Critics, then and now, question his methods, the verification of healings and his harsh public denunciations. His story also raises questions about the boundary between intense religious experience and mental illness, as his own psychiatric confinement shows.

experiences.title: The Indonesian revival (Timor, 1965)
experiences.account: Paraphrase of popular accounts: from September 1965 in the Reformed (GMIT) church at Soe, West Timor, lay evangelistic teams went out after reported visions and a sound like wind. Popular books (Kurt Koch, The Revival in Indonesia, 1970; Mel Tari, Like a Mighty Wind, 1971) reported healings, people walking across rivers, water turned to wine at communion and the dead raised. At the same time, after the failed coup of 30 September 1965 and the anti-communist killings of 1965-66, large numbers of Indonesians, especially in Java, joined churches.

primarySource.title: Kurt Koch, The Revival in Indonesia (1970); Mel Tari, Like a Mighty Wind (1971)
primarySource.citation: Koch 1970; Tari 1971; Avery T. Willis, Indonesian Revival: Why Two Million Came to Christ (1977)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Indonesian church leaders welcomed the growth; Some Indonesian church leaders later warned against exaggerated miracle claims. The government required every citizen to profess a recognised religion, which also pushed conversions.

assessments.text: The Timor accounts became famous evidence for modern 'signs and wonders' in the 1970s.
The GMIT and other churches recognised renewal but criticised sensational claims and later disorder in some teams.

Avery Willis and others attribute the Java conversions largely to political and social causes after 1965 (the killing of perhaps 500,000 alleged communists and the need to register a religion), as well as to Christian care for detainees' families.
Spectacular miracle reports, especially in Mel Tari's book, have not been independently verified and are widely treated as embellished.

experiences.story:
In 1965 Indonesia was a young republic, overwhelmingly Muslim but with significant Christian minorities, especially in eastern islands such as Timor, Sulawesi and the Moluccas. On the island of Timor, the western half then part of Indonesia, most Christians belonged to the Protestant Evangelical Christian Church in Timor (GMIT), heir to Dutch Reformed missions, and many of its members still practised traditional religious customs alongside church membership.

On the night of 30 September 1965 a group of army officers killed six generals in Jakarta in a failed coup attempt, which the army blamed on the Indonesian Communist Party (PKI). In the months that followed, army units and civilian militias killed an estimated half a million or more alleged communists across Indonesia, and the army under Suharto took power. Because atheism was associated with communism and the state required belief in God, millions of Indonesians who had been nominal Muslims or followers of local religions sought registration with a recognised religion, and many joined Christian churches, especially in Java.

At the same time, according to popular revival literature, a different kind of movement was beginning in Timor. Accounts relate that in late September 1965, during a service at a Reformed church in Soe, in the hills of South Central Timor, worshippers heard a sound like a mighty wind and some saw what looked like fire, so that people outside thought the building was burning. Many confessed sins, including the use of charms and occult practices, and burned traditional objects. Lay people, including teenagers and children, formed evangelistic teams that went out to villages across Timor and neighbouring islands, often saying they had received guidance through visions.

The movement became famous abroad through popular books. The German evangelical writer Kurt Koch, who visited Indonesia, published The Revival in Indonesia (1970), and a young man from Soe, Mel Tari, published Like a Mighty Wind (1971), which became an international bestseller. These books reported dramatic miracles: thousands healed, evangelists walking across flooded rivers, water turned into wine for communion, food multiplied, and the dead raised. They had a great influence on charismatic Christians in North America and Europe.

The more spectacular claims were soon questioned. Some missionaries, church leaders in Timor and later researchers who visited the area reported a genuine and widespread movement of repentance and evangelism, but found that particular miracle stories were difficult to verify, were told differently by local people, or had grown in the retelling. Some Indonesian church leaders warned against exaggeration and against teams who claimed special revelation. Others defended the core accounts. Historians have also noted that the killings of 1965-66 reached Timor, and that churches in Indonesia generally faced painful questions afterwards about their silence or involvement in that violence.

By the early 1970s the most intense phase in Timor had passed, but church membership across Indonesia had grown substantially. The Southern Baptist missionary Avery Willis, in a 1977 study, estimated that some two million Indonesians had joined churches in the years after 1965, the result of a combination of political pressure, social change, church care for the families of those killed or imprisoned, and religious revival.

keyMoments.text: A failed coup in Jakarta is blamed on the Communist Party, beginning a political crisis.
According to revival accounts, worshippers in a Reformed church in Soe, Timor, hear a sound like wind and see what looks like fire.
Mass killings of alleged communists sweep Indonesia, while lay evangelistic teams go out across Timor.
State pressure to profess a recognised religion pushes many Indonesians, especially in Java, into churches.
Kurt Koch publishes The Revival in Indonesia.
Mel Tari's Like a Mighty Wind popularises dramatic miracle stories worldwide.
Avery Willis estimates that about two million Indonesians joined churches after 1965.

experiences.significance: The Indonesian revival and the wider church growth after 1965 made Indonesia home to one of the largest Christian populations in Asia, and the Timor stories had a large influence on Western charismatic expectations of miracles in the 'mission field'. The episode is a key case in debates over how to verify miracle reports transmitted through popular books, and over the gap between local testimony and international retelling. It also highlights the uncomfortable link between conversion and political violence, since many joined churches amid state pressure and terror. Scholars therefore treat it as several interwoven stories: a genuine local revival, a social and political conversion movement, and a body of contested revival literature.

experiences.title: The Argentine revival and Carlos Annacondia's campaigns
experiences.account: Paraphrase of participants' and scholars' accounts: after the Falklands/Malvinas war (1982) and the return to democracy (1983), mass open-air evangelistic campaigns by the businessman-evangelist Carlos Annacondia drew huge crowds in Greater Buenos Aires and La Plata. Annacondia confronted demons directly from the platform, with people manifesting and being taken to 'spiritual intensive care' tents for deliverance; healings were reported. Other figures included Omar Cabrera and, from 1992, Claudio Freidzon, whose meetings featured holy laughter.

primarySource.title: Carlos Annacondia, Listen to Me, Satan! (1998); contemporary campaign reports
primarySource.citation: Annacondia 1998; Donald Miller & Tetsunao Yamamori, Global Pentecostalism (2007)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Argentine evangelicals experienced rapid growth in the 1980s-90s. The revival's spiritual warfare emphasis strongly influenced North American 'strategic-level spiritual warfare' teaching (e.g. C. Peter Wagner) and the Toronto Blessing through visitors.

assessments.text: Hailed as a model of revival through prayer, evangelism and deliverance; Argentine leaders became influential worldwide.
Catholic bishops were concerned about proselytism; at the same time Catholic Charismatic Renewal grew in Argentina, and the future Pope Francis built friendships with Pentecostal leaders.
Criticise 'spiritual warfare' practices and holy laughter as lacking biblical warrant.
Scholars connect growth to post-dictatorship religious freedom, urban migration and the appeal of personal empowerment.

experiences.story:
For most of the twentieth century Argentina was a strongly Catholic country in which Protestants and Pentecostals were a small minority. The military dictatorship of 1976-83 brought repression and the 'disappearance' of thousands of people. In 1982 Argentina was defeated by Britain in the war over the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas), and in 1983 democracy was restored. Many Argentines experienced this period as one of national disillusionment and openness to new sources of meaning.

Carlos Annacondia, born in 1944, was a businessman who owned a small factory making nuts and bolts in Quilmes, south of Buenos Aires. He became an evangelical Christian in 1979 at a meeting led by a visiting evangelist and soon began to preach. In 1982 he began open-air campaigns, and his campaign in La Plata in 1984, held on open ground over many weeks, drew enormous crowds and became famous across Argentina. Other campaigns followed in San Justo, Mar del Plata and many other cities.

Annacondia's meetings had a distinctive style. He preached a simple gospel message and then confronted the devil directly, shouting into the microphone 'Listen to me, Satan!' (Oíme bien, Satanás). According to participants and observers, many people in the crowd fell, screamed or manifested what they and the evangelists understood as demonic possession. Trained teams of 'stretcher bearers' carried them to a large tent behind the platform, known as the 'spiritual intensive care' unit, where volunteers prayed for their deliverance, sometimes for hours. Healings were reported, including dental fillings and other dramatic claims, and great numbers responded to the invitation to accept Christ.

Annacondia was not alone. Omar Cabrera had led a large movement, Visión de Futuro, since the 1970s with mass meetings and healing; Héctor Giménez attracted large crowds in Buenos Aires; and the Pentecostal pastor Claudio Freidzon, from 1992, led meetings marked by 'holy laughter' and falling under the Spirit after visiting healing evangelists in the United States. Freidzon's meetings influenced visitors from abroad, including the Canadian pastors John and Carol Arnott, who later hosted the Toronto Blessing. The evangelist Ed Silvoso promoted city-wide prayer and 'spiritual mapping' campaigns, such as one in Resistencia (1990).

Reactions varied. Evangelical churches that cooperated with the campaigns grew rapidly, and Argentine evangelicals grew from a small minority to around a tenth of the population by the early 2000s, according to surveys. Some Catholic bishops and the press criticised the campaigns as emotional manipulation by 'sects', and some evangelicals were uneasy about the focus on demons and the spectacular phenomena. Scholars noted the appeal of the message to working-class people in the poorer suburbs of Buenos Aires after years of political trauma and economic hardship.

North American visitors, including C. Peter Wagner of Fuller Theological Seminary, studied the Argentine revival and drew from it the teaching of 'strategic-level spiritual warfare', which held that territorial evil spirits must be identified and confronted in prayer for evangelism to succeed. This teaching became influential and controversial in the global charismatic movement during the 1990s.

keyMoments.text: Businessman Carlos Annacondia becomes an evangelical Christian and begins preaching.
Argentina's defeat in the Falklands/Malvinas war adds to national disillusionment; Annacondia begins open-air campaigns.
Democracy is restored in Argentina.
Annacondia's weeks-long campaign in La Plata draws huge crowds and makes him nationally famous.
Ed Silvoso leads a city-wide prayer and evangelism campaign in Resistencia.
Claudio Freidzon's meetings in Buenos Aires begin to feature holy laughter and falling under the Spirit.
John and Carol Arnott visit Freidzon's meetings shortly before the Toronto Blessing begins.

experiences.significance: The Argentine revival transformed Argentina's religious landscape, contributing to rapid evangelical and Pentecostal growth in a traditionally Catholic country and paralleling wider Latin American trends. It shaped global charismatic practice through its emphasis on deliverance, the 'strategic-level spiritual warfare' theology of C. Peter Wagner and others, and its connections to the Toronto Blessing. Critics, both Catholic and evangelical, have questioned its theology of territorial spirits, the risks of deliverance ministry to vulnerable people, and the reliability of miracle claims. Sociologists see it as a religious response to political trauma, economic crisis and social change in the 1980s.

experiences.title: Pentecostal beginnings in Belém and Brazil's Pentecostal growth
experiences.account: Paraphrase of Assembleias de Deus histories: two Swedish Baptist immigrants from Chicago, Gunnar Vingren and Daniel Berg, came to Belém in 1910 after a prophecy naming 'Pará'. In June 1911 Celina de Albuquerque, a member of the Baptist church where they worshipped, was reported to be the first in Brazil to speak in tongues; the Pentecostal group was expelled and formed the Apostolic Faith Mission, renamed Assembleia de Deus in 1918. Healing became a hallmark of later Brazilian Pentecostalism, from the 1950s tent crusades to the neo-Pentecostal Universal Church of the Kingdom of God (founded 1977).

primarySource.title: Histories of the Assembleias de Deus no Brasil; Gunnar Vingren's diary
primarySource.citation: Vingren, Diário do pioneiro (published 1973); R. Andrew Chesnut, Born Again in Brazil (1997)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Early Brazilian Pentecostals faced Catholic opposition and were largely poor and urban; today the Assemblies of God in Brazil is one of the largest Pentecostal bodies in the world, and evangelicals were over a fifth of Brazil's population by the 2010 census, most of them Pentecostal.

assessments.text: Brazilian Pentecostalism is a central example of the global South's 'Spirit-filled' Christianity, with healing and deliverance as means of evangelism.
Catholic bishops (e.g. at the Aparecida conference, 2007) responded to losses to Pentecostalism; Catholic Charismatic Renewal grew strongly in Brazil.
Criticise neo-Pentecostal prosperity teaching and commercialisation of healing (especially in the Universal Church).
Andrew Chesnut argues Pentecostalism grows by offering healing from the 'pathogens of poverty' (illness, alcoholism, family breakdown); Paul Freston notes its growing political influence.

experiences.story:
In the early twentieth century Brazil was overwhelmingly Catholic, with small Protestant communities founded by immigrants and missionaries. Belém, at the mouth of the Amazon in the state of Pará, was a busy port enriched by the rubber boom. Gunnar Vingren and Daniel Berg were young Swedish immigrants to the United States, both from Baptist backgrounds, who had been influenced by the Pentecostal movement spreading through the Midwest, including the ministry of William Durham in Chicago. According to Assembleias de Deus tradition, at a prayer meeting in 1910 a prophecy was given that they should go to a place called 'Pará'. Neither knew where it was until they found it in a library atlas.

The two men sailed for Brazil and arrived in Belém on 19 November 1910 with almost no money and no knowledge of Portuguese. They were welcomed into the local Baptist church, worshipping in its basement while learning the language. Berg worked in a foundry and paid for Vingren's language lessons, while also selling Bibles. They began to share their beliefs about baptism in the Holy Spirit and healing with Baptist members, holding prayer meetings in homes.

According to the church's histories, in early June 1911 a church member, Celina de Albuquerque, after days of prayer, began to speak in tongues, the first such experience recorded in the movement in Brazil, and was reportedly healed of an illness. Others followed. The Baptist pastor and leadership opposed the new teaching, and on 13 June 1911 the Pentecostal group, about eighteen people, was excluded from the church. On 18 June 1911 they began meeting separately as the Apostolic Faith Mission, the date now celebrated as the founding of the Assembleias de Deus. The name was changed to Assembleia de Deus in 1918.

The movement spread first along the Amazon and through the poor north and north-east, carried by lay members who migrated in search of work. It grew among the poor, many of them rural migrants to the cities, and faced opposition from Catholic clergy and sometimes violence from local populations. Swedish Pentecostal churches, especially Lewi Pethrus's Filadelfia church in Stockholm, sent missionaries and support. Vingren returned to Sweden in 1932 in poor health and died in 1933; Berg continued until his death in 1963. Meanwhile another Pentecostal stream, the Congregação Cristã no Brasil, had been founded in São Paulo in 1910 by the Italian immigrant Luigi Francescon, also influenced by Durham.

Healing was central from the start. In the 1950s, a second wave of Pentecostalism came with mass healing campaigns in tents and stadiums by the Foursquare Church's National Evangelisation Crusade, and new Brazilian churches such as O Brasil para Cristo (1955) and Deus é Amor (1962). From the late 1970s neo-Pentecostal churches, above all Edir Macedo's Universal Church of the Kingdom of God, founded in Rio de Janeiro in 1977, combined healing, exorcism and prosperity teaching with media empires. The sociologist R. Andrew Chesnut, studying Pentecostals in Belém itself, found that experiences of healing of illness, often related to poverty, were the main reason most converts gave for joining.

By the 2010 census, evangelicals made up about 22 percent of Brazil's population, the majority of them Pentecostal, and the Assembleias de Deus had become one of the largest Pentecostal church families in the world, with many millions of members.

keyMoments.text: In the American Midwest, Gunnar Vingren and Daniel Berg receive a prophecy directing them to 'Pará'.
Vingren and Berg arrive in Belém and join the local Baptist church.
Celina de Albuquerque becomes the first in the movement in Brazil reported to speak in tongues.
The Pentecostal group of about eighteen members is excluded from the Baptist church.
The group forms the Apostolic Faith Mission, later the Assembleia de Deus.
The church adopts the name Assembleia de Deus.
Mass healing campaigns of the National Evangelisation Crusade launch a second wave of Brazilian Pentecostalism.
Edir Macedo founds the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God in Rio de Janeiro.
The census shows evangelicals at about 22 percent of Brazil's population, mostly Pentecostal.

experiences.significance: The small group in Belém became the seed of the largest Pentecostal movement in the world by number of adherents in a single country, transforming Brazilian religion, society and politics. Brazilian Pentecostalism shows how healing, especially among the poor, has driven Pentecostal growth in the Global South, and its later neo-Pentecostal forms have exported prosperity theology and media-driven churches to Africa, Europe and beyond. Critics, Catholic and Protestant, have questioned prosperity teaching, financial practices and the growing political power of evangelical blocs in Brazil's Congress. Supporters stress the dignity, community and moral transformation these churches have brought to millions of poor Brazilians.

experiences.title: Healing and growth in Chinese house churches
experiences.account: Paraphrase of field studies and testimonies: during and after the Cultural Revolution, when public churches were closed, Protestant house-church networks grew rapidly in rural provinces such as Henan, Anhui and Zhejiang. Surveys and interviews from the 1980s-2000s repeatedly found that experiences of healing from illness, often after prayer by lay evangelists, or deliverance from spirits, were among the most common reasons given for conversion. Networks such as Fangcheng and Tanghe sent itinerant evangelists across China.

primarySource.title: Fieldwork and testimonies collected by scholars and ministries
primarySource.citation: Alan Hunter & Kim-Kwong Chan, Protestantism in Contemporary China (1993); Lian Xi, Redeemed by Fire (2010)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Chinese authorities often treated unregistered groups as illegal and sometimes labelled healing practices as 'superstition'; registered Three-Self churches tended to be more cautious about healing. Some sectarian groups arising from the same milieu (e.g. Eastern Lightning) were rejected by house churches as heretical.

assessments.text: Healing and answered prayer are read as signs of the living God's power under persecution, in line with Acts.
Often more cautious, emphasising rational faith and order, while acknowledging prayer for the sick.
Cited as among the largest examples of 'signs and wonders' evangelism in the world, though many house churches do not identify as Pentecostal.
Healing claims are hard to verify; scholars explain their importance by limited rural healthcare, folk-religious expectations and the social support of house churches. Growth estimates vary widely.

debates: Verification of healing claims and growth statistics.
Heterodox sects arising in the same networks.
experiences.story:
When the Communist Party took power in China in 1949, there were perhaps around one million Protestants and three million Catholics in the country. Foreign missionaries were expelled by the early 1950s, and Protestant churches were brought under the Three-Self Patriotic Movement, founded in 1954, which required loyalty to the new state. Leaders who refused, such as Watchman Nee and Wang Mingdao, were imprisoned. During the Cultural Revolution (1966-76) all public churches were closed, Bibles were confiscated, and believers were persecuted.

Yet Christian faith did not disappear. In villages across rural China, especially in provinces such as Henan, Anhui and Zhejiang, small groups met secretly in homes to pray, sing and read from whatever Scripture they had. Leadership passed largely to lay people, many of them women. According to later testimonies and field research, these groups often spread through networks of family and neighbours, and stories of prayer for the sick and of answered prayer played a central role.

After the death of Mao Zedong and the beginning of reforms in 1978, registered churches reopened from 1979, and the extent of the growth of Christianity became visible. Researchers and visiting Christians found that many rural communities had far more believers than before 1949. In interviews and surveys from the 1980s to the 2000s, healing was repeatedly named as one of the most common reasons for conversion: a family member's recovery from illness after prayer, often in areas where medical care was scarce or unaffordable, or deliverance from what was experienced as spirit possession. Some local studies suggested that a majority of converts in particular areas cited healing.

Large networks of unregistered house churches emerged, especially in Henan, such as the Fangcheng network associated with Zhang Rongliang, the Tanghe network (China Gospel Fellowship), and the Word of Life movement of Xu Yongze, sometimes called the 'Born Again' movement. They trained young itinerant evangelists who travelled across the country, often facing arrest, imprisonment and beatings. Their worship was fervent, with tears, extended prayer and expectation of signs and wonders, and some networks developed a vision, known as 'Back to Jerusalem', of sending missionaries westward across Asia.

The state's response varied over time and region. Unregistered groups were often treated as illegal gatherings, and officials sometimes condemned healing practices as 'superstition' or 'illegal medical practice'. Registered Three-Self churches were generally more cautious about healing and charismatic practices. The same environment also produced groups regarded as heretical by house churches and the state alike, such as Eastern Lightning (the Church of Almighty God), founded in the early 1990s, which teaches that Christ has returned as a Chinese woman and which house-church networks accused of infiltrating and kidnapping their leaders.

Estimates of the total number of Protestants in China vary widely, from around 23 million in official surveys to 60 million or more in some outside estimates. Scholars such as Alan Hunter, Kim-Kwong Chan and Lian Xi have stressed that this growth took place largely without missionaries, through Chinese lay leadership and a popular Christianity that emphasised prayer, healing and the experience of God's power in daily life.

keyMoments.text: The Communist Party takes power; missionaries are soon expelled.
The Three-Self Patriotic Movement is established to bring Protestant churches under state supervision.
The Cultural Revolution closes all public churches; believers meet secretly in homes.
Registered churches begin to reopen, revealing extensive growth in rural Christianity.
The state issues its policy on religion (Document 19), allowing limited registered worship while unregistered groups remain vulnerable.
Large house-church networks in Henan send itinerant evangelists across China; healing testimonies feature prominently in their growth.
Leaders of several house-church networks issue a joint confession of faith to clarify their orthodoxy against heretical sects.

experiences.significance: The growth of Chinese house churches is one of the most remarkable developments in modern Christian history, producing one of the world's largest Protestant populations under a hostile state and without foreign missionary leadership. It shows how healing and experiences of spiritual power can drive conversion in contexts of poverty and limited medical care, a pattern also seen in Africa and Latin America. Critics and scholars point to the difficulty of verifying healing claims and growth statistics, the vulnerability of such networks to heretical sects, and the tensions between registered and unregistered churches. Their story remains central to debates about church and state, religious freedom and indigenous Christianity in China.
